questions.q: What is missing from the method below for production?
questions.hint: What happens if the SMS service is slow? And how will you know if it fails?

options.text: There is no timeout: if the SMS service is slow, the request will hang for a long time
options.why: If you don't set one, HttpClient waits up to PHP's default_socket_timeout (usually 60 seconds), and the worker stays stuck that whole time.

options.text: If it fails, there is no log to tell you which order's SMS didn't go out
options.why: Without catching the exception and writing a log with order_id, nobody can tell later whose SMS was lost.

options.text: It should have used GET instead of POST
options.why: Sending an SMS causes a change; GET is only for reading. POST is right.

options.text: It should call json_encode() by hand instead of using the json option
options.why: The json option encodes for you and sets the correct Content-Type, which is the usual way.

questions.q: A parcel-booking request to the courier's API times out after 3 seconds. What should the code assume now?
questions.hint: Can you tell apart "the request arrived" and "the response got lost on the way"?

options.text: The parcel wasn't booked, so resend with a new key
options.why: It may have been booked and only the response failed to come back. With a new key the courier treats it as a new parcel, and two get booked.

options.text: The outcome is unknown, so retry with the same idempotency key
options.why: Seeing the same key, the courier knows it is a repeat of the earlier request, so however many times you send it, there is one parcel.

options.text: The parcel is booked, so carry on without a tracking code
options.why: The request may never have arrived. If you assume it did, the customer waits for a parcel that was never booked.

options.text: Ask the customer to place the whole order again
options.why: This pushes the system's uncertainty onto the customer, and it also raises the risk of duplicate orders.

questions.q: Which of these are part of making an endpoint production-ready?
questions.hint: Recall the seven questions. Which one answers none of them?

options.text: Returning a clear 422, not a 500, on bad input
options.why: This answers "what if the input is wrong?": the mistake is caught at the door.

options.text: Writing a log with order_id on failure
options.why: This answers "how will we know when it goes wrong?": without context you can't search a log for anything.

options.text: Adding as many design patterns and interfaces as possible
options.why: The number of patterns answers none of the seven questions, and needless layers only make code harder to read.

options.text: Keeping a way to switch the new behavior off with a feature flag
options.why: This answers "how do we get back if it goes bad?": you can stop bad code without a new deploy.

questions.q: Sarah's PR got 30 comments, all about names and whitespace. After the merge it turned out there was no permission check, so anyone could cancel someone else's order. What should change in the process?
questions.hint: A reviewer's attention is limited. Where did it get spent?

options.text: Add two more reviewers to every PR
options.why: If everyone looks in the same wrong order, even five people will get stuck on the style they notice first. It just takes longer.

options.text: Hand style to a linter, and have reviewers look at design, failure and security, in that order
options.why: When a machine handles style, human attention goes to the costly mistakes, and the checklist order brings up the permission question first.

options.text: Drop reviews and rely only on automated tests
options.why: The author never thought of the path whose test is missing, so they never wrote it. Catching a missing permission check takes another pair of eyes.

options.text: Ask for style comments to come last, and keep everything else as is
options.why: If people look at style, their attention is used up there. It needs to move wholly to machines, and the other steps need an order too.

questions.q: Jake used to collect the current request's data in a static array in PHP, and it never caused a problem. What happens if he takes the same habit to a Node.js service?
questions.hint: What does PHP-FPM do when a request ends, and what does a Node process do?

options.text: Nothing: the behavior is the same in both
options.why: PHP-FPM wipes memory at the end of every request; a Node process stays alive. The behavior is completely different.

options.text: Data will stay across requests, and memory will keep growing
options.why: In Node, module-level variables are shared by all requests. One user's data can be seen by another, and the array never gets emptied.

options.text: Node will empty the array by itself at the end of each request
options.why: The garbage collector won't touch anything that still has a reference, and a module-level variable always has one.

options.text: TypeScript will catch the mistake at compile time
options.why: This isn't a type error, it is a lifetime error. To the compiler the code is perfectly valid.

questions.q: Ryan's 1,800-line PR has been sitting for two days and nobody is reviewing it. What is the best step?
questions.hint: Put yourself in the reviewer's seat: which PR would you open first?

options.text: Have the manager pressure someone into approving it quickly
options.why: Under pressure the reviewer will skim and approve, and the whole point of a review is lost.

options.text: Merge it yourself and hope someone looks at it later
options.why: "Looking later" after a merge almost never happens, and by then the mistake is already in production.

options.text: Split the work into small, independent PRs, each with a clear description
options.why: A PR of 200-400 lines gets reviewed fast and carefully, and with a description the reviewer reads the code knowing its purpose.

options.text: Add the remaining features to this PR as well and finish in one go
options.why: The bigger the PR, the longer the review waits, and the less likely it is that mistakes get caught.

questions.q: An endpoint that succeeded every time on a laptop broke in production. What is the most likely reason?
questions.hint: Which situations never came up on the laptop?

options.text: There are more users in production, so adding server RAM will fix it
options.why: RAM stops none of these: bad input, double clicks or a hanging outside call.

options.text: On the laptop only the good-day path ran: slow APIs, bad input and double clicks never came up
options.why: Running alone, only the happy path is exercised. In production the other paths happen every day, and the code had no preparation for them.

options.text: Production must be running an older PHP version
options.why: It could be, but that would show in the very first minute after a deploy. Here it breaks only in particular situations, not all the time.

questions.q: `/api/orders` takes 1.4 seconds. What do you do first?

options.text: Rewrite the serializer
options.why: That is a guess; starting big work without measuring can waste a week.

options.text: Measure with the Profiler/Stopwatch where the time goes
options.why: Once you know the bottleneck, one change in the right place gives a big gain.

options.text: Add more server RAM
options.why: Adding hardware without knowing the cause raises the cost and leaves the real problem.

options.text: Put a cache in front
options.why: It hides a slow query without fixing it, and cache invalidation brings new problems.

questions.q: The Profiler's Doctrine tab shows the same query 300 times. What is the likely cause?
questions.hint: Loading a list and then fetching each item's relation separately.

options.text: N+1: a separate query for every item in the list
options.why: This is what lazy loading inside a loop looks like. Use `JOIN FETCH` or a batch query.

options.text: A slow database connection
options.why: A slow connection would make one query slow, not run it 300 times.

options.text: A missing index
options.why: Without an index one query is slow; the count doesn't become 300.

questions.q: What does the EXPLAIN ANALYZE output below tell you?
questions.code:
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..18334.00 rows=1 width=64)
                    (actual time=0.02..1180.4 rows=50 loops=1)
  Filter: (customer_id = 42)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 999950
questions.hint: It read nearly 1 million rows to find 50.

options.text: It reads the whole table and filters; `customer_id` needs an index
options.why: Seq Scan and Rows Removed by Filter at 999950: with an index it would go straight to the rows it needs.

options.text: The query is fine, nothing needs to change
options.why: 1180ms is far too long for a simple lookup.

options.text: The table has few rows, so it is fast
options.why: It had over 1 million rows; saying it has few is wrong.

questions.q: Which statements about a spike are correct?
questions.hint: What is the real product of a spike?

options.text: Its purpose is to answer one specific question
options.why: If the question isn't clear, the spike loses direction.

options.text: The time is boxed (for example 1-2 days)
options.why: Otherwise the spike grows into a whole project.

options.text: You can write the code carefully and move it straight into production
options.why: Spike code is untested and rushed; in production it becomes debt.

options.text: It is enough to report the result as "it worked"
options.why: You need to write down the numbers (time, memory) and the decision.

questions.q: Ryan measured on his new development laptop with 100 rows and said "the query is fine, 2ms". Production has 10 million rows. What is the problem?
questions.hint: How does a Seq Scan feel on small data?

options.text: On small data it is fast even without an index; the problem will appear on big data
options.why: Slowness grows with data size. You need to measure on production-sized data.

options.text: The laptop's CPU is fast, so the measurement is wrong
options.why: It is the data size that makes the difference, not the CPU.

options.text: There is no problem
options.why: A number from 100 rows doesn't predict how 10 million rows will behave.

questions.hint: Dev mode, one run, the average, many changes at once: which of these are mistakes?

options.text: Measuring on production-sized data, in prod mode (APP_DEBUG=0)
options.why: In debug mode Symfony does extra work, and the numbers get distorted.

options.text: Running several times and looking at p95
options.why: A single run is full of noise; p95 catches the slow share.

options.text: Making five optimization changes at once and then measuring
options.why: You can't tell which one worked.

options.text: Looking only at the average response time
options.why: The average hides the slowest few percent.

questions.q: In a new project you are asked to look into "refund emails aren't going out". What is the best first step?
questions.hint: Not the whole code, one specific path.

options.text: Read every file in the `src/` folder from the start
options.why: The order of the files isn't the path of the work; it takes a long time and you can't pick out the part that matters.

options.text: Find the refund route or command, and follow one request from there
options.why: Starting from an entry point means reading only the files of that job.

options.text: Change the email-sending code and see what happens
options.why: Change before understanding and you touch the wrong place.

options.text: Call the previous developer and ask for a full explanation
options.why: First build your own map and a specific question; then asking a colleague saves time.

questions.q: Which command tells you which listeners run when `App\Event\RefundIssued` happens?
questions.hint: An event and its listeners: which debug command?

options.text: php bin/console debug:router
options.why: It lists URLs and controllers, not events.

options.text: php bin/console debug:event-dispatcher App\Event\RefundIssued
options.why: It shows every listener on that event, in priority order.

options.text: php bin/console debug:autowiring
options.why: It shows the list of types you can autowire.

options.text: php bin/console about
options.why: It shows the Symfony version and the environment.

questions.q: The code has a strange `usleep(500000)`, with a comment saying "to avoid the gateway rate limit". What is the best thing to do now?

options.text: Trust the comment and leave it alone
options.why: The comment may be out of date; the gateway's rules may have changed since.

options.text: Read why it was added with `git blame` and `git show`, and check whether it is still needed
options.why: History tells you the reason, and running it or testing it shows the truth today.

options.text: Delete it straight away
options.why: Delete it without knowing and the rate limit may start failing again.

questions.q: Which of these are good ways to understand an unfamiliar codebase?
questions.hint: Entry points, running it, history, a map.

options.text: Run `php bin/phpunit --testdox` and read the list of behaviors
options.why: Test names describe the code's expected behavior in plain language.

options.text: Draw a one-page map of entry points, services, data and dependencies
options.why: Drawing shows you the gaps in your understanding.

options.text: Assume what each class does from its name
options.why: Names can mislead; check against the code or the debug commands.

options.text: Start a big refactor before you understand it
options.why: Refactor without understanding and you break behavior.

questions.q: Which of these questions does `debug:messenger` answer?

options.text: Which controller a URL runs
options.why: That is `debug:router`.

options.text: Which handler exists for which message class
options.why: It shows the messages and their handlers for each bus.

options.text: Which parameters a service receives
options.why: That is `debug:container`.

questions.q: What belongs on a one-page map?
questions.hint: From entry to data, and what you don't know.

options.text: The entry points and the main services
options.why: Where work comes in and where the real rules live is the core of the structure.

options.text: Where the data lives and the outside dependencies
options.why: Failures usually happen at the boundary with data and outside systems.

options.text: Every method of every file
options.why: A map that detailed stops being a map; the 3-5 main parts are enough.

options.text: The questions you still haven't understood
options.why: The list of questions is the basis for your next investigation and for asking a colleague.
